records.source: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν;
records.gloss: What then will we say?
pieces: What then are we to say?

R.1: So what should we say about this?

decisions.choice: a question that opens the next step of the argument
decisions.reason: Paul asks what follows from what he has just said: that where sin increased, grace increased all the more (5:20). He uses the same question in 4:1, 8:31 and 9:14.

records.heading: Dead to sin, alive to God

records.source: ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;
records.gloss: Shall we continue in the sin, that the grace may abound?
pieces: Are we to stay on in sin, so that grace may increase all the more?

L.1: Should we remain in sin, so that grace may increase?

R.1: Should we keep living in sin, so that God can show even more of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace?

decisions.reason: Paul had said that where sin increased, grace increased even more (5:20). Someone could twist that into a reason to go on sinning. Some were already accusing Paul of teaching "let us do evil so that good may come" (3:8).

decisions.choice: remain in: go on living in sin as in a place one stays
alternatives: continue in the practice of sinning
decisions.reason: epimenō is to stay on or persist. With "in sin" it pictures sin as the place or power a person lives under, which verse 2 takes up: "how will we still live in it?"

decisions.choice: sin: the power, not single acts
decisions.reason: The Greek has "the sin", with the article, as all through 5:12-21 and this chapter. Sin is pictured as a power that reigns, enslaves and pays wages (5:21, 6:6, 6:23).

decisions.choice: so that God can show even more of his grace
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the giver of grace, which the Greek leaves understood.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· οἵτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ;
records.gloss: Not may it be; who died to the sin, how still shall we live in it?
pieces: Certainly not! We are people who died to sin; how could we still be living in it?

L.2: May it not be! We who died to sin, how will we still live in it?

R.2: Of course not! We have died to sin. So how could we keep on living in it?

decisions.reason: mē genoito, "may it not happen", is Paul's strongest way of rejecting a false conclusion (3:4, 3:6, 6:15, 9:14, 11:1).
Balanced and Readable use ordinary English for an emphatic no, as 3:4 and 9:14 do. "God forbid" adds a word for God that the Greek does not have.

decisions.choice: died to sin: our life under sin's rule has ended
decisions.reason: To die to something is to be finished with it, beyond its reach. The death meant is the believer's share in Christ's death (verses 3-6). It does not say believers no longer feel the pull of sin; verses 12-13 still urge them not to let it reign.

decisions.choice: who: people of such a kind
decisions.reason: hoitines often means "people who are such that". The point is what kind of people believers are: people who have died to sin.

records.source: ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι ὅσοι ἐβαπτίσθημεν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν εἰς τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ ἐβαπτίσθημεν;
records.gloss: Or are you unaware that as many as were baptized into Christ Jesus into the death of him were baptized?
pieces: Or have you not grasped that everyone among us who was baptized into {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus was baptized into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death?

L.3: Or are you unaware that as many [of us] as were baptized into {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus were baptized into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death?

R.3: Surely you know that when we were baptized and joined to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus, we were also joined to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death.

decisions.choice: baptized into Christ Jesus: brought into union with him
decisions.reason: To be baptized "into" someone is to be joined to him and to belong to him (Galatians 3:27; 1 Corinthians 10:2, "baptized into Moses"). Joined to Christ, the believer is joined to what happened to him, his death first of all.

decisions.choice: or: a reminder of what they should already know
decisions.reason: Paul asks whether they have missed what their baptism meant. The question assumes they know it, as in 7:1.
Readable says what "baptized into" means: joined to Christ and to his death. It keeps "baptized" once, so the act itself is still named.
Readable turns the question into a statement, since Paul expects the answer yes.

records.source: συνετάφημεν οὖν αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος εἰς τὸν θάνατον, ἵνα ὥσπερ ἠγέρθη Χριστὸς ἐκ νεκρῶν διὰ τῆς δόξης τοῦ πατρός, οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς περιπατήσωμεν.
records.gloss: We were buried with therefore him through the baptism into the death, that just as was raised Christ out of dead [ones] through the glory of the Father, so also we in newness of life should walk.
pieces: So through baptism we were buried with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} into death, in order that, as {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might live a life that is new.

L.4: Therefore we were buried with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} through baptism into death, so that just as {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was raised from [the] dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.

R.4: When we were baptized, it was as if we were buried with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and shared {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death. {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was raised from the dead by the glorious power of the Father. In the same way, we too are to live a completely new life.

decisions.choice: into death goes with baptism: the baptism that joins us to his death
alternatives: buried ... into death (death as the place of burial)
decisions.reason: The words "into death" pick up verse 3, "baptized into his death". The burial is the sign that the death was real; it is through baptism that believers share it.

decisions.choice: the glory of the Father: his glorious power
decisions.reason: God's glory is the shining out of who he is. Here it is his power at work in raising Jesus, as "glory" and "power" stand side by side in Colossians 1:11 and 2 Thessalonians 1:9.
To "walk" is a Hebrew way of speaking of how a person lives day by day. "Newness of life" is a life of a new kind, the life of the age to come begun now.
Balanced and Readable say what "walk" means. Literal keeps the picture.
Readable makes clear that the burial is shared through baptism, not literally.
Readable joins "glory" to the power it means here (see the meaning decision on the glory of the Father).

records.source: Εἰ γὰρ σύμφυτοι γεγόναμεν τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐσόμεθα·
records.gloss: If for united we have become in the likeness of the death of him, but also of the resurrection we will be;
pieces: For if we have grown into one with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the likeness of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death, we will certainly be one with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the likeness of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} resurrection as well.

L.5: For if we have become united with the likeness of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death, we will certainly also be [united with the likeness] of [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] resurrection;

R.5: We have become one with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by going through something like {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death. So we will surely become one with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by going through something like {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rising to life too.

decisions.reason: symphytos is used of things that grow together, like a graft that becomes one with the plant. It describes a close and living union.

decisions.choice: united with him by the likeness of his death
decisions.reason: The Greek can mean "united with the likeness of his death" or "united with him in the likeness of his death". Verses 4 and 8 speak of dying and living with Christ, so the union is with him, and the likeness is the way believers share his death, through baptism (verse 4). Literal keeps the Greek's shorter form.

decisions.choice: we will be: a sure future, already at work now
decisions.reason: The future may point to the resurrection of the body at the end (8:11) or to the new life that follows from the believer's union with Christ now (verse 4). Verse 8 also uses the future. Both are likely in view; the words are left as a future.

decisions.choice: [united with the likeness] (L); be one with him in the likeness (B)
decisions.reason: The second half of the Greek leaves the words of the first half to be understood. Literal supplies them in brackets, Balanced in full.
Balanced keeps the growing picture in symphytos.

decisions.choice: going through something like his death / his rising to life
decisions.reason: Readable explains "likeness" and says "rising to life" for resurrection.

records.source: τοῦτο γινώσκοντες ὅτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη, ἵνα καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας, τοῦ μηκέτι δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ὁ γὰρ ἀποθανὼν δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
records.gloss: this knowing that the old of us self was crucified with, that might be done away with the body of the sin, [for] the no longer to be enslaved us to the sin; \v 7 the [one] for having died has been justified from the sin.
pieces: We know this: our old self was nailed to the cross with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, so that the body of sin would be stripped of its power and we would no longer serve sin as slaves.
For anyone who has died is declared free from sin.

L.6: knowing this, that our old self was crucified with [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}], so that the body of sin might be made powerless, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin;
L.7: for the one who has died has been justified from sin.

R.6: We know that the people we used to be were put to death on the cross with {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. This happened so that the self that sin ruled would be put out of action, and we would no longer be slaves to sin.
R.7: Anyone who has died is free from sin's claim.

decisions.choice: our old self: the person we were under sin's rule
decisions.reason: The "old self" is not a part of a person but the whole person as he or she was in Adam, before being joined to Christ (5:12-21; Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9).

decisions.choice: the body of sin: the self under the rule of sin
decisions.reason: The body is the person as one who lives and acts in the world. "Of sin" says who has been ruling it. The body itself is not evil; verse 13 urges believers to give its parts to God.

decisions.choice: made powerless: put out of action
decisions.reason: katargeō means to make ineffective, to take out of use. The old order of sin loses its hold, though verses 12-13 show the struggle is real.

decisions.choice: justified from sin: declared free from sin's claim
alternatives: set free from sin (without the legal sense)
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in Romans dikaioō means God declares people righteous (3:24, 5:1). Here, with "from sin", it has a legal sense: as death ends a person's debts and legal claims, the one who has died with Christ is acquitted and released from sin's claim. It may also echo a saying that death settles all accounts.

decisions.choice: declared free (B); free from sin's claim (R)
decisions.reason: Here dikaioō means acquittal and release, not being counted righteous, so Balanced says "declared free" and Readable "free from sin's claim" instead of the usual "declared righteous".

decisions.choice: the people we used to be
decisions.reason: Readable explains "old self" in plain words.

decisions.choice: put to death on the cross with Christ
decisions.reason: Readable names Christ, whom the Greek leaves understood, and explains "crucified with".
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: slavery to sin, set against being freed from it (6:7).

records.source: εἰ δὲ ἀπεθάνομεν σὺν Χριστῷ, πιστεύομεν ὅτι καὶ συζήσομεν αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: If now we died with Christ, we believe that also we will live with him;
pieces: Now if we died along with {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, we believe we are also going to share in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} life.

L.8: Now if we died with {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, we believe that we will also live with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}};

R.8: We died together with {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. Because of that, we believe we will live together with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} too.

decisions.choice: if: a condition taken as true
decisions.reason: Paul is not doubting that believers died with Christ; he has just said so (verses 3-6). The "if" sets out the ground for what follows.

decisions.choice: we will live with him: now and at the resurrection
decisions.reason: As in verse 5, the future tense may point to life with Christ after the resurrection, or to the new life that follows now (verse 11, "living to God"). The words are left as a future.
Readable states the condition as a fact, because it is one Paul takes as true.
Balanced says "share in his life" for the single Greek verb "live with".

records.source: εἰδότες ὅτι Χριστὸς ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν οὐκέτι ἀποθνῄσκει, θάνατος αὐτοῦ οὐκέτι κυριεύει·
records.gloss: knowing that Christ having been raised out of dead [ones] no longer dies, death of him no longer rules;
pieces: For we know that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, once raised from the dead, does not die any more; death is no longer {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} master.

L.9: knowing that {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, having been raised from [the] dead, no longer dies; death no longer rules over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.9: We know that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was raised from the dead and cannot die again. Death has no power over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} anymore.

decisions.choice: death no longer rules over him
decisions.reason: Death is pictured as a ruler (5:14, 5:17). Christ was under its power when he died, but his resurrection was not a return to a life that ends in death again, as with Lazarus; it was victory over death itself.
kyrieuō, "be lord over", is rendered "master" so that the picture of a ruler is kept without sounding like a title of Christ.

records.source: ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανεν, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ· ὃ δὲ ζῇ, ζῇ τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: That which for he died, to the sin he died once for all; that which but he lives, he lives to the God.
pieces: When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died to sin once and for all; and now that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives for God.

L.10: For [the death] that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died to sin once for all; but [the life] that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives to God.

R.10: When {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} died, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died to sin's power once and for all. The life {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives now, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} lives for God.

decisions.choice: he died to sin: he was finished with sin's power
decisions.reason: Christ never sinned (2 Corinthians 5:21). He died to sin in that he came under its power, which brings death, and by his death he left that power behind for good. Sin has no more claim on him.

decisions.choice: once for all: one time, never to be repeated
decisions.reason: ephapax means both "once" and "once and for all time", as Hebrews uses it of Christ's sacrifice (Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10).

decisions.choice: lives to God: lives for God and in relation to him
decisions.reason: The dative "to God" matches "to sin": his life belongs wholly to God.
Readable says "sin's power" so that no reader thinks Christ himself sinned.

records.source: οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς λογίζεσθε ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι νεκροὺς μὲν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ζῶντας δὲ τῷ θεῷ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
records.gloss: So also you consider yourselves to be dead indeed to the sin, living but to the God in Christ Jesus.
pieces: In the same way, you also are to count yourselves as dead to sin, and as living for God in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

L.11: So also you, count yourselves to be dead to sin, but living to God in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.11: In the same way, you must think of yourselves as dead to sin's power but alive for God, because you belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus.

decisions.reason: logizesthe can be a statement ("you count") or a command ("count"). After "so also you" it is most naturally a command, and verses 12-13 go on with commands.

decisions.choice: count: reckon as true, put to the account
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of God counting faith as righteousness in chapter 4. Believers are to treat as true what God has done.
Many later manuscripts add "our Lord" at the end, probably from verse 23. Early witnesses do not have it, and the SBLGNT ends with "Christ Jesus". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.
The same English as chapter 4, so the link to God's counting is kept.

decisions.choice: because you belong to Christ Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable explains "in Christ Jesus", as Romans 9:1 and 12:5 do.

records.source: Μὴ οὖν βασιλευέτω ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐν τῷ θνητῷ ὑμῶν σώματι εἰς τὸ ὑπακούειν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις αὐτοῦ, μηδὲ παριστάνετε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν ὅπλα ἀδικίας τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἀλλὰ παραστήσατε ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ ὡσεὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ζῶντας καὶ τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν ὅπλα δικαιοσύνης τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: Not therefore let reign the sin in the mortal of you body for the to obey the desires of it, \v 13 neither present the members of you [as] weapons of unrighteousness to the sin, but present yourselves to the God as from dead [ones] living and the members of you [as] weapons of righteousness to the God.
pieces: So do not let sin reign as king in your mortal body, making you obey its desires.

Do not keep handing over the parts of your body to sin as weapons for wrongdoing. Instead, hand yourselves over to God, as people who were dead and are now alive, and hand over the parts of your body to God as weapons for righteousness.

L.12: Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires,
L.13: and do not present your members [as] weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but present yourselves to God as [people] living from [the] dead, and your members [as] weapons of righteousness to God.

R.12: So do not let sin rule like a king in your body, which will one day die. Do not let sin make you do whatever your body craves.
R.13: Do not give any part of your body to sin to use as a weapon for doing wrong. Instead, give yourselves to God, since you were dead and now you are alive. Give every part of your body to God to use as a weapon for righteousness.

decisions.reason: autou is neuter and goes with "body", not with sin. Sin rules by making people do what the mortal body craves.
The body is still mortal; the resurrection of the body is still to come (8:11, 8:23). That is why sin can still try to rule in it.
hoplon can mean a tool of any kind, but in Paul it means weapons (13:12; 2 Corinthians 6:7, 10:4). The picture of sin as a ruler who wages war and pays wages (verse 23) fits weapons.

decisions.choice: do not go on handing over (present); hand yourselves over (aorist)
decisions.reason: The first command is in the present tense and forbids a habit; the second is aorist and calls for a decisive act of handing oneself to God.

decisions.choice: members: the parts of the body
decisions.reason: The "members" are the body's parts and abilities, hands, feet, tongue and eyes, through which a person acts.
Balanced and Readable say "parts of your body" for "members", which today means members of a group.
Readable explains "mortal".
adikia is the opposite of righteousness. Balanced and Readable use plain words; Literal keeps "unrighteousness" so the contrast with "righteousness" shows.

records.source: ἁμαρτία γὰρ ὑμῶν οὐ κυριεύσει, οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν.
records.gloss: Sin for of you not will rule, not for you are under law but under grace.
pieces: Sin will not be lord over you, for you do not live under the law but under grace.

L.14: For sin will not rule over you, for you are not under [the] law but under grace.

R.14: Sin will not have power over you, because you no longer live under the rule of the law. You live under the rule of God's grace.

decisions.reason: The future is a promise, not a command: sin will not be master, and the reason follows.

decisions.choice: under law: under the law of Moses as the order one lives by
decisions.reason: To be "under" something is to live under its rule (3:19, Galatians 3:23-25, 4:4-5). The law is good (7:12), but it could not break sin's power; it made sin plain and even gave it opportunity (5:20, 7:8). Grace now rules instead (5:21).
Balanced keeps the sense of kyrieuō, "be lord over", which sets sin's claim against the Lord's (verse 23).
Readable explains "under".

records.source: Τί οὖν;
records.gloss: What then?
pieces: What then?

decisions.reason: Readable spells out the short question, as in 3:9.

records.heading: Slaves of righteousness

records.source: ἁμαρτήσωμεν ὅτι οὐκ ἐσμὲν ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν;
records.gloss: Shall we sin because not we are under law but under grace?
pieces: Should we go ahead and sin, since we live under grace and not under the law?

L.15: Should we sin because we are not under [the] law but under grace?

R.15: Since we are not ruled by the law but by God's grace, does that mean we can go ahead and sin?

decisions.reason: Verse 1 asked about staying in sin (present tense). This question uses the aorist: may we commit sins, since the law no longer condemns us?

decisions.choice: under grace and not under the law
decisions.reason: Balanced puts grace first, the stronger term, so the question ends on what was given up.
Readable names God as the giver of grace.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο·
records.gloss: Not may it be;
pieces: Certainly not!

decisions.reason: mē genoito, "may it not happen", is Paul's strongest way of rejecting a false conclusion (3:4, 3:6, 6:15, 9:14, 11:1).
Balanced and Readable use ordinary English for an emphatic no, as 3:4 and 9:14 do. "God forbid" adds a word for God that the Greek does not have.

records.source: οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ᾧ παριστάνετε ἑαυτοὺς δούλους εἰς ὑπακοήν, δοῦλοί ἐστε ᾧ ὑπακούετε, ἤτοι ἁμαρτίας εἰς θάνατον ἢ ὑπακοῆς εἰς δικαιοσύνην;
records.gloss: Not know you that to whom you present yourselves [as] slaves for obedience, slaves you are to whom you obey, whether of sin to death or of obedience to righteousness?
pieces: Surely you know this: if you put yourselves at someone's disposal as slaves, ready to obey, then you belong as slaves to the one you obey. That master is either sin, bringing death, or obedience, bringing righteousness.

L.16: Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves [as] slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin [leading] to death, or of obedience [leading] to righteousness?

R.16: You know that if you give yourselves to someone and promise to obey, you become slaves of the one you obey. If you obey sin, you are its slaves, and that leads to death. If you choose obedience, you are its slaves, and that leads to righteousness.

decisions.reason: In the Roman world a free person could sell himself or herself into slavery, for instance to pay a debt. Whoever did so belonged to the master and had to obey.

decisions.choice: obedience leading to righteousness: a right life now and God's verdict at the end
decisions.reason: Set against "death", righteousness here is the outcome of obeying: a life that is right with God, ending in his final verdict of acquittal and life (verses 22-23). It is not earned by obedience; the obedience is the obedience of faith (1:5).
Balanced turns the question into a statement, since Paul expects the answer yes.

decisions.choice: That master is (B); If you obey sin / If you choose obedience (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek names the two masters in a short phrase; Balanced and Readable supply the words that link them back to "slaves".
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: slavery to sin set against obedience; the whole passage turns on whose slave one is.

records.source: χάρις δὲ τῷ θεῷ ὅτι ἦτε δοῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὑπηκούσατε δὲ ἐκ καρδίας εἰς ὃν παρεδόθητε τύπον διδαχῆς, ἐλευθερωθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἐδουλώθητε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ·
records.gloss: Thanks but to the God that you were slaves of the sin, you obeyed but from heart to which you were handed over form of teaching, \v 18 having been set free and from the sin, you were enslaved to the righteousness;
pieces: But God be thanked! Once you were slaves of sin, yet you gave wholehearted obedience to the pattern of teaching into whose care you were handed.
Freed from sin, you were made slaves of righteousness.

L.17: But thanks [be] to God that you were slaves of sin, but you obeyed from [the] heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,
L.18: and having been set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

R.17: But thank God! You were once slaves of sin. But then you obeyed with all your heart the teaching God placed you under.
R.18: You were set free from sin, and now you are slaves of righteousness.

decisions.reason: charis here is thanks given to God, as in 7:25 and 1 Corinthians 15:57, not grace given by him.

decisions.choice: thanks that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed
decisions.reason: Paul is not thankful that they were slaves of sin. The two clauses go together: thanks be to God that they were slaves of sin but obeyed.

decisions.choice: handed over to the pattern of teaching
decisions.reason: One would expect "the teaching handed over to you" (as in 1 Corinthians 15:3). Paul turns it round: they were handed over to the teaching, like slaves passed to a new master. The "pattern" (typos) is the shape of the gospel teaching that now forms their lives. The passive implies that God handed them over.
The aorist passive "you were enslaved" describes what happened when they were freed from sin: no one is without a master, and their new master is righteousness.
Balanced uses an exclamation for the short Greek thanksgiving.

decisions.choice: the teaching God placed you under
alternatives: the teaching to which you were handed over
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who handed them over, which the passive implies.
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: slaves of sin set against being freed from sin.

records.source: ἀνθρώπινον λέγω διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν· ὥσπερ γὰρ παρεστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ καὶ τῇ ἀνομίᾳ εἰς τὴν ἀνομίαν, οὕτως νῦν παραστήσατε τὰ μέλη ὑμῶν δοῦλα τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ εἰς ἁγιασμόν.
records.gloss: Human I speak because of the weakness of the flesh of you; just as for you presented the members of you slaves to the impurity and to the lawlessness for the lawlessness, so now present the members of you slaves to the righteousness for sanctification.
pieces: I am putting this in everyday human terms because of your natural human weakness. Just as you once handed over the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, which only led to more lawlessness, so now hand them over as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.

L.19: I speak in human [terms] because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members [as] slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, [leading] to lawlessness, so now present your members [as] slaves to righteousness, [leading] to sanctification.

R.19: I am using a picture from everyday life because you are only human and these things are hard to grasp. You used to give the parts of your body as slaves to impure living and to lawless living, and the lawlessness kept growing. Now give them as slaves to righteousness, so that you will become holy.

decisions.choice: I speak in human terms: I use an everyday picture
decisions.reason: Paul apologizes for the picture of slavery. Being "slaves of righteousness" is not the whole truth about life with God, which is freedom (8:15, 8:21), but the picture helps.

decisions.choice: the weakness of your flesh: human limitation
decisions.reason: Flesh here is human nature in its weakness. The weakness may be of understanding, so that a plain picture is needed, or of moral strength, so that a strong one is needed. Either way it is ordinary human frailty, not the flesh set against the Spirit as in chapter 8.
hagiasmos is the process or state of being set apart to God and made holy. It is the outcome of serving righteousness, as death is the outcome of sin (verses 21-22).

decisions.choice: natural human weakness (B); you are only human (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "flesh" means here, plain human frailty, instead of "flesh", which in Romans often means human nature under sin.
Balanced and Readable use everyday words for hagiasmos; Literal keeps "sanctification".
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: slavery to impurity set against slavery to righteousness, in the passage on freedom from sin.

records.source: Ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ.
records.gloss: When for slaves you were of the sin, free you were to the righteousness.
pieces: Back when sin owned you as slaves, you were free, as far as righteousness was concerned.

L.20: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.

R.20: When you were slaves of sin, you did not have to answer to righteousness at all.

decisions.choice: free with regard to righteousness: righteousness was not their master
decisions.reason: The dative means "free as far as righteousness goes". The freedom was no real freedom: it was the freedom of slaves who did not serve righteousness, and its end was death (verse 21).

decisions.choice: did not have to answer to
decisions.reason: Readable explains the irony of "free" in plain words.
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: slaves of sin, "free" from righteousness.

records.source: τίνα οὖν καρπὸν εἴχετε τότε ἐφ’ οἷς νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε;
records.gloss: What therefore fruit had you then in the [things] of which now you are ashamed?
pieces: So what fruit did you get back then from the things that now make you ashamed?

L.21: What fruit then did you have at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed?

R.21: What good did you get back then from doing the things that now make you ashamed?

decisions.choice: one question: what fruit came from the things you are now ashamed of
alternatives: What fruit did you have then? Things you are now ashamed of.
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads the whole verse up to here as one question. Some read the question as ending after "then", with the answer "things you are now ashamed of". The sense is much the same.
Fruit is what a life produces. Verse 22 takes up the same word for the life given to God.
Readable says what "fruit" means here.

records.source: τὸ γὰρ τέλος ἐκείνων θάνατος·
records.gloss: The for end of those [things] [is] death.
pieces: Those things end in death.

L.21: For the end of those things [is] death.

R.21: In the end, those things bring death.

decisions.choice: end: the goal and final outcome
decisions.reason: telos is the point a thing comes to, its result. Death is not only a penalty added from outside but where that way of life leads (verse 23).

alternatives: The end of those things is death.
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the noun "end" into a verb.

records.source: νυνὶ δέ, ἐλευθερωθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας δουλωθέντες δὲ τῷ θεῷ, ἔχετε τὸν καρπὸν ὑμῶν εἰς ἁγιασμόν, τὸ δὲ τέλος ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: Now but, having been set free from the sin, having been enslaved but to the God, you have the fruit of you to sanctification, the and end life eternal.
pieces: Now, though, freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have fruit that leads to holiness, and its outcome is eternal life.

L.22: But now, having been set free from sin and having been enslaved to God, you have your fruit [leading] to sanctification, and the end [is] eternal life.

R.22: But now you have been set free from sin, and you have become God's slaves. What you get from this is a holy life, and in the end you will have eternal life.

decisions.choice: but now: the new situation since they believed
decisions.reason: "But now" sets the present against "then" in verse 21, as in 3:21 and 7:6.

decisions.choice: eternal life: the life of the age to come
decisions.reason: Eternal life is the life of God's new age, without end, given in full at the resurrection (2:7, 5:21).
As in verse 19.
Readable says what "fruit" means here.
"Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: freed from sin and made slaves of God: the contrast with freedom is the point.

records.source: τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: The for wages of the sin [is] death, the but gift of the God [is] life eternal in Christ Jesus the Lord of us.
pieces: The wages sin pays are death, but God's free gift is eternal life in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

L.23: For the wages of sin [is] death, but the gift of God [is] eternal life in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

R.23: Sin pays out death as its wages. But God gives eternal life as a free gift to everyone who belongs to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus our Lord.

decisions.reason: opsōnion was the pay or ration money of a soldier, and then any wage. It fits the picture of sin as a ruler with weapons at its service (verse 13). Sin pays what is earned; God gives what is not earned.
charisma is a gift given freely, out of grace (5:15-16). It stands against wages, which are owed.

decisions.choice: in Christ Jesus our Lord: in union with him
decisions.reason: Eternal life is found in Christ and given to those who belong to him, as in 5:21 and 8:1-2.
Balanced and Readable add "free" to bring out the contrast with wages.
Readable explains "in Christ Jesus", as in verse 11.
